newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein to open Jordan's parliament Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein to open Jordan's parliament Tuesday.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan opens a new session of parliament on Tuesday just days after extending an olive branch to critics of his government's tough economic policies and opponents of his two-year peace with Israel.
But the Islamist-dominated parliamentary opposition has pledged to have no dealings with a government which it says has ignored Jordan's poor and failed to stand up to Israel.

Tuesday's session, which kicks off the final parliamentary season before 1997 elections, is the first since the king suspended parliament's summer session three months ago in the face of violent protests against bread price rises in August.

The monarch, who blamed the riots on foreign agitation and vowed to respond with an iron fist, has since made a flurry of conciliatory gestures. Last week he ordered the release of all remaining protesters, offering them "a fresh start".

"Dialogue has been, and will continue to be our most ideal option to achieve progress for the country and its citizens," the king said in a letter to Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti ordering the detainees to be set free.
He also announced an amnesty for prisoners who had not "harmed national security" and told Kabariti to lower the price of bread, a vital food for most of Jordan's 4.2 million people.

A few days earlier the king gave a lift home from jail to his fiercest critic, Laith Shubailat, who was serving a three-year prison sentence for branding the monarch a traitor for his 1994 peace treaty with Israel.

Since the last parliamentary session the king, seen as Israel's closest Arab friend, has warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of a return to violence unless he remains faithful to Israel's accords with Arabs.

But the king's moves have done little to defuse opposition anger with a government which it accuses of bulldozing an unpopular agenda -- peace with Israel, a cold shoulder to Iraq, and tough economic reforms -- over public sentiment.
Leading Islamist deputy Bassam al-Amoush said the government had failed to follow up the king's tougher line on Israel.
"The Jews have broken the agreements...The king attacked (Netanyahu's) Likud Party, but the government have done nothing," he told Reuters.
"The people of Jordan are suffering," he said, referring to the government's IMF-backed economic reforms. "Prices are higher, there is more poverty.
"The government is living in a crisis," he said. "The next session cannot be successful if it continues."

But businessmen, cheered by what they see as the government's commitment to difficult economic reforms, say they are looking for speedy passage in parliament of three laws aimed at trade and business liberalisation.
The proposed legislation includes revisions to customs and companies laws aimed at making Jordan more investor friendly, and a law introducing greater transparency in the Amman stock exchange.
